item.content:encoded:
European Space Agency's Hera probe reveals stadium-sized crater from NASA asteroid test

Category: Science

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has revealed that NASA’s 2022 impact test carved a crater spanning nearly the full width of Dimorphos, a 151-meter asteroid moonlet, and left it tumbling chaotically around its larger companion, Didymos. Hera’s first close-up images also show hundreds of boulders around the pair; neither asteroid poses a threat to Earth [7][4][9]. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) shortened Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos by 33 minutes, but scientists had not seen the collision’s physical effects in detail. Hera’s measurements are intended to show how the asteroid’s shape, mass and structure affected the deflection and help refine predictions for future impact missions [7][13][5]. Hera is surveying the asteroids from about 25 to 30 kilometers away. The European Space Agency (ESA) plans to move Hera closer in December 2026 and deploy two CubeSats in January 2027; one is designed to use radar to examine Dimorphos’s interior [7][6][31].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once!

— Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator (European Space Agency)

Did you know: Didymos’s surface gravity is about 40,000 times weaker than Earth’s, according to Hera team member Naomi Murdoch [9].

Key Points

  • Uneven damage: Hera’s images show little apparent change to the boulder fields on the side of Dimorphos opposite the impact, despite the crater across the struck face [7][20].
  • Boulder hazard: The newly observed rocks range from tens of centimeters to several meters, and their origin—impact debris or material already in the system—has not been established [24][30][9].
  • Image resolution: Hera's first close-up imagery resolved features at about 2.7 meters per pixel [36][1].
  • DART benchmark: NASA had defined a reduction of at least 73 seconds in Dimorphos’s orbital period as a successful test; the measured change was about 33 minutes [8][3].
  • Surface composition: Italy’s Milani CubeSat is tasked with examining the asteroid’s surface composition and surrounding dust [7][29][31].

Perspectives

Ian Whittaker, a physics lecturer at Nottingham Trent University, cautioned that predicting a deflection is not straightforward because the result depends partly on how much material an asteroid ejects when struck [13].

Sources: The Guardian

Timeline

  • 26 September 2022: NASA’s DART spacecraft deliberately struck Dimorphos in a deflection test [7][4].
  • 7 October 2024: ESA launched Hera to study the aftermath of the DART collision [10][13].
  • 4 November 2026: Hera reached the Didymos system after its two-year journey [17].
  • 7 November 2026: Hera photographed the asteroid pair from about 29 kilometers away [36].
  • 25 November 2026: ESA released Hera’s first close-up images of the impact site [7][4].
  • December 2026: Hera is scheduled to approach to roughly 13 kilometers from the asteroids [7][6].
  • January 2027: Hera plans to deploy two CubeSats for closer asteroid studies [7][31].

Technical Details

  • Momentum transfer: Measuring Dimorphos’s mass alongside its observed orbital change will help researchers estimate how efficiently DART transferred momentum, including the contribution of ejected material [31][13].
  • Hera instruments: The spacecraft’s Asteroid Framing Camera records monochrome images, Hyperscout H observes in 25 spectral bands, and JAXA’s Thermal Infrared Imager measures surface temperature [7][42].
  • Close-range radar: The Juventas CubeSat is designed to use low-frequency radar to probe the asteroid’s interior, a measurement that could constrain its internal structure [7][31].

Scientific Significance

  • Impact physics: DART’s mass, speed and trajectory were known, and Hera’s images can be compared with pre-impact views, giving researchers an unusual dataset for studying impacts at asteroid scale [13].
  • Rubble-pile behavior: Dimorphos is thought to be an aggregate of smaller rocks held together by extremely weak gravity, making its response to an impact harder to predict than that of a solid body [8].
  • System-wide effects: DART changed not only Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos but also the binary pair’s orbit around the Sun [2].

Historical Background

The collision destroyed DART, and impact debris obscured the site from the accompanying LICIACube spacecraft. By the time the dust cleared, LICIACube had departed, leaving Hera to document the crater directly [8][31].

item.title: Army says Iowa blast produced no detectable airborne lead; testing continues
item.author: Kite Feed Generator (Science / Environmental Science)
item.description: The U.S. Army says air monitors detected no airborne lead after it detonated the nation’s stockpile of degraded lead azide Wednesday at its Iowa ammunition plant. Officials later lifted the shelter-in-place order for nearby residents [6][15][27]. The blast destroyed 68 barrels of the explosive, which the Army said had become unstable in storage and could detonate without warning [3][26]. The initial air readings are not the final environmental assessment. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said it would review soil-sampling results before deciding whether further public-health advice is needed. The Army and Federal Emergency Management Agency said more testing and updates would follow [15][27]. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said it had collected more than 1,200 air, land and water samples before the blast and would continue monitoring. NASA deployed research aircraft and used its space-based TEMPO pollution instrument to collect environmental and atmospheric data, while independent researchers planned further testing. Laboratory analysis of environmental samples is expected to take days to weeks, Purdue University environmental engineering professor Andrew Whelton said [15][9][27].

The initial air readings are not the final environmental assessment. The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services said it would review soil-sampling results before deciding whether further public-health advice is needed. The Army and Federal Emergency Management Agency said more testing and updates would follow [15][27]. The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear

— Rob Sand, Iowa governor-elect (Scientific American)

Key Points

  • NASA monitoring: NASA deployed a P-3 Orion, a Gulfstream III and a B200 research aircraft, and used its space-based TEMPO pollution instrument to observe the event [9][10].
  • Follow-up guidance: Whelton said eventual recommendations could differ among communities based on distance from the detonation area and whether they were upwind or downwind [27].

Perspectives

U.S. Army: Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley called the operation successful and said mitigation measures reduced the risk to nearby residents to as close to zero as possible [15].

Sources: Nebraska Examiner

Rob Sand, Iowa governor-elect: Sand called for immediate transparency about how the crisis developed and said officials should continue testing before expressing certainty about its effects [26][6].

Sources: The Guardian

Iowa environmental groups: The groups argued that lead settling on land or entering waterways could expose people, livestock and wildlife even after airborne dust dissipates [13][25].

Sources: Newsday

Timeline

  • March 2026: An Army inspection found that the stored lead azide had partially crystallized [3]
  • 23 November 2026: A federal appeals court ruling put the detonation back on track, and the Army set the blast for Wednesday [3][16]
  • 25 November 2026: The Army carried out the blast; officials later issued an all-clear [6][27]

Historical Background

The national stockpile was transferred to the Iowa ammunition plant in 2009 and retained for possible future use [3][12]. The military had moved away from using lead azide because of its sensitivity and handling risks [7]. An earlier disposal in Colorado in 1977 left 75% of lead particulate at the site without mitigation, according to Army explosives expert Col. Aaron Teller [1].

Action Items

  • Follow local health guidance on lead exposure: The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services advised residents to follow their health care providers’ routine lead-testing recommendations and contact providers if they suspect exposure [15].

item.content:encoded:
Pakistan's Zeeshan Ali becomes first foreign astronaut aboard China's Tiangong station

Category: Science

Pakistan Air Force pilot and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has entered China’s Tiangong space station, becoming the first foreign astronaut to visit the outpost and the first Pakistani to reach orbit. Shenzhou-24 docked on Nov. 25 after launching from Jiuquan, China, carrying Ali, Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi. The flight is the first joint mission with a foreign astronaut in China’s crewed space program [1][5][8][3]. Ali is assigned four China-Pakistan research projects in biotechnology and materials, including tests involving photosynthetic cyanobacteria, quinoa seeds and composite materials. The mission includes more than 90 experiments and technology tests in fields including life sciences, materials science, physics and space medicine [12][13][25]. Ali is expected to spend five days to a week aboard Tiangong, then return to Earth with two members of the Shenzhou-23 crew aboard their spacecraft. Chinese astronauts Tang and Wu are scheduled to remain for the usual six-month rotation, while Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will stay for a year as researchers study how prolonged spaceflight affects the human body [2][19][18].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

What comes after this flight matters more than the flight itself

— Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Pakistani astronaut and payload specialist (The Nation)

Did you know: Pakistani adventurer Namira Salim flew on Virgin Galactic’s suborbital Galactic 04 mission in October 2023, before Ali became the first Pakistani to reach orbit [4][1].

Key Points

  • Research range: Fundamental-physics work will use optical-lattice quantum simulation to explore new states of matter and test a space cold-atom interferometer for inertial measurement [12].
  • Crew milestone: Tang Hongbo is set to become the first astronaut to visit Tiangong three times [12].
  • Training demands: Ali trained in Beijing for seven months, including intensive Chinese-language instruction because spacecraft controls, software and voice announcements operate in Chinese [2][11].
  • Station capacity: Tiangong can host up to six astronauts during crew handovers, allowing Shenzhou-24’s arrival to overlap with the departing crew [8].

Perspectives

Blaine Curcio, space industry consultant: Curcio said sending another country’s astronaut requires substantial trust and gives Pakistan detailed insight into China’s crewed space program. He said the mission could show other countries that Beijing is open to similar cooperation [2].

Sources: The Guardian

Ahsan Iqbal, Pakistan's planning minister: Iqbal said the flight could lead to expanded cooperation, including a possible joint lunar mission. He said it shows how developing countries can build capabilities in strategically important areas [8].

Sources: The Citizen

Timeline

  • February 2025: China and Pakistan signed a spaceflight cooperation agreement [4][7]
  • April 2026: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud were selected for training [21]
  • 24 November 2026: Chinese officials announced the three-person Shenzhou-24 crew [12]
  • 25 November 2026: Shenzhou-24 launched from Jiuquan and docked with Tiangong [1][8]

Scientific Significance

  • Life-support research: The microalgae experiment examines whether photosynthetic microorganisms could provide oxygen and nutrients for future long-duration missions. The flight tests the idea in orbit but will not establish its practical performance [13][16].
  • Seed response: Researchers will test how microgravity and cosmic radiation affect quinoa seeds to learn about seed longevity and traits that may withstand harsh environments. The articles describe planned experiments, not results [13][3].
  • Space medicine: Crew studies will include multi-omics research and studies of behavior and brain function, alongside tests of health-maintenance technologies [12].

Historical Background

China-Pakistan space cooperation dates to the early 1990s; China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover is scheduled to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028 [2][8].

Q&A

Q: Could other countries send astronauts to Tiangong?

A: Space industry consultant Blaine Curcio said Brazil and Egypt may seek opportunities, though future participation would depend on available partnerships. He also said European countries or others participating in the International Space Station could become candidates if no Western replacement station is available [12][2].

item.description: A federal judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early review of eight broadcast licenses held by Disney-owned ABC, ruling that the network is likely to show the FCC retaliated against it for speech critical of President Trump [3][5]. item.content:encoded:
Judge blocks FCC’s early review of eight Disney-owned ABC station licenses

Category: Business

A federal judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early review of eight broadcast licenses held by Disney-owned ABC, ruling that the network is likely to show the FCC retaliated against it for speech critical of President Trump [3][5]. The preliminary injunction pauses the review while ABC and Disney’s lawsuit proceeds; U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan also rejected the FCC’s bid to dismiss the case [6][10]. The FCC ordered the stations to seek early renewals in April, although their licenses were not due for renewal until 2028 at the earliest. The agency said its action related to an investigation of Disney’s diversity and employment practices. AliKhan found that the timing, public statements by Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, and the potential loss of licenses supported ABC’s retaliation claim [5][16][20]. AliKhan did not bar the FCC from taking other future actions against ABC, saying she could not issue a blanket injunction against unspecified threats [5][20]. The FCC said it disagreed with the decision and expects to prevail; the lawsuit will continue [10][14].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

Chairman Carr has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders

— U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan (NPR)

Did you know: Judge AliKhan counted 11 public calls by President Trump over two years for the FCC to strip ABC’s licenses, with the latest in July 2026 [3][16].

Key Points

  • Business exposure: ABC’s owned stations serve six of the 10 largest U.S. markets, including New York, Los Angeles and Houston, and contribute significantly to the network’s bottom line [3].
  • Editorial changes: ABC said pressure had affected its editorial choices: “The View” stopped inviting political candidates ahead of the 2026 elections, and a Senate candidate’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” interview appeared on YouTube rather than broadcast television [3][6].
  • FCC rationale: The commission said it accelerated the review because it was investigating whether Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices violated anti-discrimination rules. It said Disney had not adequately answered its information requests [3][20].
  • Narrow injunction: AliKhan barred further steps in the early license-renewal proceedings but denied ABC’s request to prohibit any other formal or informal FCC actions aimed at influencing editorial discretion [5][11].
  • FCC response: The FCC called the ruling wrong on the facts and the law and said it would continue using its authority to enforce broadcasters’ public-interest obligations [10][9].

Perspectives

Federal Communications Commission: The agency maintains that the review arose from its investigation into Disney’s diversity and employment practices, not ABC’s programming, and says broadcasters must meet public-interest obligations [20][10].

Sources: CBS News

ABC and Disney: The companies argued the early review itself caused irreparable First Amendment harm by forcing broadcasters to weigh independent editorial decisions against the risk of losing valuable licenses [20].

Sources: CBS News

Anna M. Gomez, FCC commissioner: The commission’s sole Democratic member said the ruling should prompt broadcasters facing pressure to defend their rights rather than capitulate [3][19].

Sources: NPR

Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press: President Bruce Brown called the decision a win for all broadcasters, arguing that the case was novel because of the administration’s punitive actions [11].

Sources: Deadline

Timeline

  • March 2025: FCC opened an investigation into Disney’s employment practices [6]
  • 28 April 2026: FCC ordered ABC stations to file early license-renewal applications [12]
  • August 2026: ABC and Disney sued to block the early review [10]
  • 6 October 2026: Judge heard arguments and requested supplemental briefs on alternatives available to the FCC [10]
  • 25 November 2026: AliKhan issued an injunction halting the early license review [5][3]

Historical Background

FCC broadcast licenses ordinarily run for up to eight years, with renewal dates staggered by station location [16]. Before the April 2026 order, the agency had not ordered an early review of this kind in more than 50 years, and the stations’ scheduled renewals were not due before October 2028 [13][17].

Business Angle

  • The license review could have put ABC stations in major markets at risk; the stations contribute significantly to the network’s bottom line [3].
  • The injunction is preliminary, and the judge declined to restrict other potential FCC actions [5].
  • ABC said regulatory pressure had affected its candidate bookings and program distribution before any license was revoked [3][6].
